title: Datadog LLM observability: instrumentation and spans

opening.headline: When the app is functioning normally but LLM traces are not visible in Datadog, learners acquire the method of separately inspecting the monitoring path and the transmission path.
body: The app responds normally and the LLM call succeeds, yet on the Datadog LLM Observability dashboard, there are no traces. Possible causes include: the metrics may not have been collected, the metrics may have been collected but failed to transmit, or the metrics may have been transmitted but accumulated under a different app name.

In this class, we distinguish between the measurement path that creates spans and the transmission path that sends them to Datadog. We examine how to measure using the Datadog SDK, the meaning of environment variables, differences between agent-based and agentless approaches, how to connect using OpenTelemetry, and various types of spans. We also walk through a case study where we read environment variables one by one to narrow down the root cause.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Datadog LLM Observability's SDK metrics, OpenTelemetry integration, and span types can be explained.
Can analyze whether measurements or transmissions have been lost by reading environment variables and code.

screens.title: LLM traces are not visible in Datadog
screens.lead: First, let's examine the scenario where it's unclear where to begin checking when tracing is not visible. Read through, considering what might be broken in each section of the diagram.

visual.alt: In the flow from measurement and transmission in the app to the Datadog screen, the final screen shows an empty diagram.

paragraphs: The app responds normally, and the LLM call succeeds. However, the Datadog LLM Observability screen shows no traces. In such cases, potential causes are scattered across various possibilities: the instrumentation might not have occurred, instrumentation might have occurred but transmission was blocked, or traces might have been sent under a different app name.

Here is an important distinction: the measurement path of how a span is created and the transmission path of how data is sent to Datadog are separate issues. Mixing these two can lead you to suspect every setting at once, making it difficult to narrow down the root cause.

Note that the Datadog documentation also introduces this product as Agent Observability. In this course, the same product is referred to using both names. The objective of this course is to develop the ability to examine both paths separately.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: The symptom of no traces appears equally in both measurement and transmission issues. Since the symptoms alone cannot distinguish between these two, consider how to differentiate them within the configuration. Follow along with the lesson.

screens.outro: First, let's recall how the two transmission paths differ.

screens.title: Do you know the difference between agent-based and agentless approaches?
screens.lead: When you select a path box, the instructor's thought process is displayed. Since you haven't entered an answer yet, first consider whether the values used for authentication are the same or different across the two paths before clicking.

items.prompt: Path 1: Sends data to Datadog via the Datadog Agent running on the same host from the app
items.answer: The app sends data created using the SDK to the Datadog Agent running on the same host, which then forwards it to Datadog. In this case, the app does not need to store its API key directly. Authentication is handled by the Agent.

items.prompt: Path 2: The app sends directly to Datadog without an Agent
items.answer: This is a method used in environments where placing an agent is not possible. Since the SDK directly sends data to Datadog, the application must know its own API key and the destination URL to send data to.

items.prompt: Are the authentication values the same for both paths?
items.answer: Yes. In the agent-based approach, the agent handles authentication, so the app does not need an API key; in the agentless approach, the SDK directly sends the request, thus requiring an API key. This difference is fundamental when reading environment variables in the subsequent screen.

screens.outro: Now, we will check the differences between the two methods by reading environment variables one at a time.

screens.title: SDK Measurement: Reading environment variables and code, with Agent and agentless approaches
screens.lead: Compare how agent-based and agentless methods differ in terms of commands and required values by alternately selecting between the two states. Pay attention to where the changing lines are.

visual.alt: A diagram comparing the two paths by which data reaches Datadog—agent-based and agentless approaches.
labels: The API key is handled by the Agent.

states.label: Agent-based approach
states.body:
In an environment with the Datadog Agent, execute as follows:

```
DD_SITE=datadoghq.com DD_LLMOBS_ENABLED=1 DD_LLMOBS_ML_APP=qa-bot ddtrace-run python app.py
```

Reading the line works as follows: `DD_LLMOBS_ENABLED=1` enables LLM observability data transmission. `DD_LLMOBS_ML_APP` specifies the application name used to group traces; if not specified, it defaults to the `DD_SERVICE` value. `DD_SITE` indicates the Datadog site to which data will be sent. `ddtrace-run` wraps the application to enable automatic tracing. The SDK supports Python, Node.js, Java, and Go (experimental), and provides both automatic and manual tracing APIs. The default value for `DD_LLMOBS_SAMPLE_RATE` is 1.0, representing the proportion of traces to preserve. If misconfigured, it appears as follows: if ENABLED is missing, the span itself is not created, and if ML_APP differs from expectations, traces are stored under a different application name.

states.label: Agentless approach
states.body:
In an environment without an agent, the same command adds two values together.

``
DD_SITE=datadoghq.com DD_API_KEY=$DD_API_KEY DD_LLMOBS_ENABLED=1 DD_LLMOBS_AGENTLESS_ENABLED=1 DD_LLMOBS_ML_APP=qa-bot ddtrace-run python app.py
```

`DD_LLMOBS_AGENTLESS_ENABLED=1` declares that no agent is being used. This setting is only required when no agent is present, and in that case, the SDK handles the transmission directly, making `DD_API_KEY` necessary only at that time. It can also be enabled programmatically by calling `LLMObs.enable(ml_app="qa-bot", agentless_enabled=True)`, and it should not be used together with `ddtrace-run`. If both site and api_key are omitted, the values of the DD_SITE and DD_API_KEY environment variables are used. If they don't match, you'll see an error indicating that there is no transmission path when no agent is present, and data will not arrive if the key and site values do not align.

screens.outro: Having read about measuring using the SDK, let's now compare the approach of connecting using OpenTelemetry without an SDK.

screens.title: SDK Metrics and OpenTelemetry Integration
screens.lead: Compare how the two length options for creating a span differ when selecting each tab. Pay attention to the required packages and settings, as well as authentication values.

tabs.label: SDK Measurement
tabs.body: You begin tracing with the Datadog SDK. For Python, install the `ddtrace` package, and for Node.js, install `dd-trace`. Run your app with `ddtrace-run` or call `LLMObs.enable` in your code to enable tracing. For providers supported by automatic tracing, spans are created without additional code, while spans are manually created using the tracing API where needed.

tabs.label: OTel Connection
tabs.body: This is the path of directly sending traces from an application measured using OpenTelemetry without the Datadog SDK or Datadog Agent. You only need a Datadog API key and an OpenTelemetry generative AI semantic convention version 1.37 or higher, or a span that adheres to the supported OpenInference convention. Set the OTLP protocol to `http/protobuf` and specify the endpoint and `dd-api-key`, `dd-otlp-source=llmobs` headers via environment variables.

tabs.label: Which path to take?
tabs.body: If your application is already using OpenTelemetry or leverages OpenTelemetry instrumentation from a specific framework, an OTel integration is natural. If you want to broadly utilize Datadog features and prefer automatic instrumentation, using the SDK-based instrumentation is more convenient. Regardless of the approach, the way spans are created differs, but traces visible in Datadog follow the same span type hierarchy.

screens.outro: Since both lengths follow the same span type system, let's now organize the span types.

screens.title: span and trace, and span types
screens.lead: The following table lists the seven types of spans recognized by Datadog LLM Observability. Review each row to determine which types can serve as root spans.

data.caption: Span types and root span feasibility
rows: A single operation to invoke an LLM
A predefined sequence of operations including LLM calls and surrounding tasks
A service that retrieves pages, processes the text, and generates summaries
A dynamic sequence of operations that determines the model's next action
A factor involving external program or service calls made by an LLM
Web search API or calculator call
An independent step without external service calls
Data preprocessing before sending the prompt
A model or function call that returns an embedding
A search operation to retrieve documents from an external knowledge base
A call that retrieves ranked documents from a vector database
data.notes: A span is a unit of work, and a trace is a collection of nested spans that process a single request. The root span is the first span in a trace and marks both the start and end of the trace. Embedding and Retrieval are subcategories of Tool.

screens.outro: Now, let's analyze a real-world incident based on the environment variables you've read so far.

screens.title: Case Explanation: Missing omission caused by API key absence in agentless mode
screens.lead: The instructor works through a case with no traces step by step. Select the next arrow to follow the process of separately inspecting the measurement path and transmission path.

visual.alt: An app, SDK, Datadog trio connected, with the flow stopping in a section lacking a key.

steps.title: Situation: Deployed to serverless, but no traces are available
steps.body: Deployed in a serverless environment without an agent using the following environment variables: `DD_LLMOBS_ENABLED=1`, `DD_LLMOBS_ML_APP=qa-bot`, `DD_LLMOBS_AGENTLESS_ENABLED=1`, `DD_SITE=datadoghq.com`. There are four lines. The app responds normally, but Datadog shows no traces.

steps.title: Step 1: Measurement verification - Is a span being created?
steps.body: First, verify from the measurement path. If records indicate that LLMObs is activated and a span has been created, then the measurement path is normal. In this case, since `DD_LLMOBS_ENABLED=1` is present, the measurement is considered enabled.

steps.title: Step 2: Transmission Confirmation: Read one line at a time
steps.body: Next, we verify the transmission path. Since there is no agent, AGENTLESS must be enabled, and since transmission is direct, `DD_API_KEY` and `DD_SITE` must actually be injected into the environment. We compare the lines one by one. AGENTLESS is enabled and SITE is present.

steps.title: Step 3 Cause: DD_API_KEY is not reduced
steps.body: The list does not contain `DD_API_KEY`. The SDK is attempting to send data directly to Datadog, but the receiving side cannot authenticate whose data it is. Even though the metrics are normal, transmission is blocked at the sending stage, and nothing appears on the screen.

steps.title: Step 4 Distinction: Same symptoms, different causes
steps.body: The same symptoms can have different causes. If the activation setting itself is absent, it's a measurement issue; if activation is enabled but the key is missing, it's a transmission issue. Since symptoms alone cannot distinguish between these cases, the fastest approach is to read environment variables one by one.

steps.title: Step 5: Revision and Follow-up Verification
steps.body: Inject `DD_API_KEY` into the deployment configuration. After recovery, if the expected screen is not displayed, verify the app name and sampling settings. Check whether the `DD_LLMOBS_ML_APP` value matches the expected app name, and whether `DD_LLMOBS_SAMPLE_RATE` matches the expected rate. If the app name does not match, the data will be accumulated under a different app.

steps.title: Conclusion: Reading in parallel halves the range.
steps.body: By separating the measurement path from the transmission path and reading environment variables, the root cause scope is halved. Since the loss of a single authentication value can block the entire transmission, it is necessary to verify that all required values are present, even if most values appear to be correct.

screens.outro: Having completed the example, I will now summarize the core concepts.

screens.title: Key Takeaway: Verify the measurement path and transmission path separately.
screens.lead: We organize the course content into a single review sequence. Begin by recalling the initial scene's blank screen and read through it.

paragraphs: When traces are not visible, first split the paths into two. The measurement path is the route that creates a span, while the transmission path is the route that sends data to Datadog. The path that creates spans includes Datadog SDK instrumentation and OpenTelemetry integration, and each path requires different configurations. The OTel path is possible with just spans that follow Datadog's API key and specification, without requiring a SDK or agent.

In the transmission path, first check whether an Agent is present. If an Agent is present, authentication is handled by the Agent; if not, enable agentless mode and match the API key and site. If the app name differs, the entries will be stacked under a different app, so also verify `DD_LLMOBS_ML_APP`.

The traces displayed on the screen are categorized by span type. There are seven types: LLM, Workflow, Agent, Tool, Task, Embedding, and Retrieval. Among these, only LLM, Workflow, and Agent can serve as root spans. Finally, remember to read environment variables line by line to determine whether a measurement or transmission has been delayed.

callout.label: Check sequence
callout.text: First, check if measurement is enabled; next, based on agent presence, verify whether it's AGENTLESS with the correct API_KEY and SITE; finally, confirm that the ML_APP name matches expectations.

checks.intro: Just check the environment variables you just read. Results are not recorded.
checks.q:
In agentless serverless, after deploying with the following environment variables, there are no traces in Datadog. What value is missing?  
DD_LLMOBS_ENABLED=1  
DD_LLMOBS_ML_APP=qa-bot  
DD_LLMOBS_AGENTLESS_ENABLED=1  
DD_SITE=datadoghq.com
options: DD_LLMOBS_SAMPLE_RATE — Not specified, it is not transmitted
DD_SERVICE — if missing, ml_app becomes empty and transmission is blocked
ddtrace-run — if this line is present, environment variables are not needed
DD_API_KEY — in agentless mode, the SDK sends it directly, so an authentication key is required.
checks.explain: In agentless mode, the SDK sends data directly to Datadog, so an API key is required. Even if monitoring is enabled, data transmission will be blocked if no API key is provided.

wrong.0: SAMPLE_RATE is preserved by default at 1.0 even if it is not explicitly specified.
wrong.1: The ml_app is designated as DD_LLMOBS_ML_APP, therefore DD_SERVICE is not required.
wrong.2: ddtrace-run is a command wrapper and does not replace environment variable configuration.

checks.intro: Check the span type rules. The results are not recorded.
checks.q: Which span type in Datadog LLM Observability cannot be a root span?
checks.explain: LLM, Workflow, Agent can become root spans, but Tool, Task, Embedding, Retrieval cannot.

wrong.0: A workflow can serve as the root that encapsulates an entire set of tasks in a predefined sequence.
wrong.1: An agent can serve as the root of a flow that determines the next action of a model.
wrong.3: LLM span belongs to the types that can become root spans.

glossary.def: A feature that enables verifying LLM app traces, spans, and evaluations in Datadog, also introduced in the document as Agent Observability.
This is a method where the SDK sends data directly to the API key without the Datadog Agent.
This is the app name that bundles all traces and spans from the same LLM application.
This is a classification that distinguishes the nature of operations performed by spans such as LLM, Workflow, Agent, Tool, Task, Embedding, and Retrieval.
The first span of a trace indicates the start and end of the trace.

misconceptions.myth: If traces are not visible, measurement has not been taken.
misconceptions.fact: Measurement occurs, but incorrect transmission settings are also common. The measurement path and transmission path must be separately verified to determine the cause.

misconceptions.myth: The Datadog SDK is required to send data via OpenTelemetry.
misconceptions.fact: OTel tracing is possible without the Datadog SDK or Agent. Simply having an API key and a span that adheres to either Generative AI semantic specification 1.37 or above, or an OpenInference specification supported by the system is sufficient.

misconceptions.myth: All span types can become root spans.
misconceptions.fact: Only LLM, Workflow, and Agent can be root. Tool, Task, Embedding, and Retrieval cannot be root.

misconceptions.myth: If most environment variables match, partial data is displayed.
misconceptions.fact: The transmission can be blocked even if one authentication value is missing. Even if most values appear correct, each required value must be verified line by line.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: The measurement path and transmission path are different issues and should be verified separately.
SDK instrumentation and OpenTelemetry integration follow different paths to create spans.
If no agent is available, enable agentless mode and configure the API key and site.
The span types are LLM, Workflow, Agent, Tool, Task, Embedding, and Retrieval, and only the first three can serve as roots.
It reads environment variables one line at a time to determine whether measurements or transmissions have been lost.
